questions.knowledge_point: Solving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
questions.problem:
Find the general solution to the equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}-3x{y}^{′}+5y=0,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={x}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $x$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {x}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda -2}-3x\cdot \lambda {x}^{\lambda -1}+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){x}^{\lambda }-3\lambda {x}^{\lambda }+5{x}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {x}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +5] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-3\lambda +5 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +5 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-4\lambda +4)-4+5 & =0 \\ (\lambda -2)^{2} & =-1 \\ \lambda -2 & =\pm \text{i} \\ \lambda  & =2\pm \text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =2\pm \text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{x}^{2+\text{i}} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)), \\ {x}^{2-\text{i}} & ={x}^{2}{e}^{-\text{i}\operatorname{ln}⁡x}={x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution to our equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =A{x}^{2+\text{i}}+B{x}^{2-\text{i}} \\  & =A{x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))+B{x}^{2}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)) \\  & =(A+B){x}^{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+\text{i}(A-B){x}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can rewrite $y(x)$ as

$$
y(x)={x}^{2}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\operatorname{ln}⁡x))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
questions.problem:
Find the solution to the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}-9t{y}^{′}+41y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=1,\,t>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
Note that the given equation is an instance of the Cauchy-Euler equation. So, we assume that the solutions take the form $y={t}^{\lambda }.$ Differentiating $y$ with respect to $t$ gives

$$
{y}^{′}=\lambda {t}^{\lambda -1},\,{y}^{″}=\lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}.
$$

Substituting the above to our differential equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{2}\cdot \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda -2}-9t\cdot \lambda {t}^{\lambda -1}+41{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ \lambda (\lambda -1){t}^{\lambda }-9\lambda {t}^{\lambda }+41{t}^{\lambda } & =0 \\ {t}^{\lambda }[\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +41] & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}\lambda (\lambda -1)-9\lambda +41 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

We solve the auxiliary equation by completing the square:

$$
\begin{aligned}{\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +41 & =0 \\ ({\lambda }^{2}-10\lambda +25)-25+41 & =0 \\ (\lambda -5)^{2} & =-16 \\ \lambda -5 & =\pm 4\text{i} \\ \lambda  & =5\pm 4\text{i}\end{aligned}
$$

Hence, the roots are $\lambda =5\pm 4\text{i}.$

Now, we note that

$$
\begin{aligned}{t}^{5+4\text{i}} & ={t}^{5}{e}^{\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)), \\ {t}^{5-4\text{i}} & ={t}^{5}{e}^{-\text{i}4\operatorname{ln}⁡t}={t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the general solution is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(t) & =A{t}^{5+4\text{i}}+B{t}^{5-4\text{i}} \\  & =A{t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t))+B{t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\text{i}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)) \\  & =(A+B){t}^{5}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+\text{i}(A-B){t}^{5}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t).\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we can rewrite the expression for $y(x)$ as follows:

$$
y(t)={t}^{5}({c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t))
$$

where ${c}_{1}=A+B$ and ${c}_{2}=\text{i}(A-B).$  

Now let's find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}.$

Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

We now need to apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=1.$ First, we substitute ${c}_{1}=1$ and  differentiate $y$ to find ${y}^{′}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(t) & ={t}^{4}((5{c}_{2}-4)\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+(4{c}_{2}+5)\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t))\end{aligned}
$$

Substituting ${y}^{′}(1)=1$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}1 & =4{c}_{2}+5 \\ -4 & =4{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)={t}^{5}(\operatorname{cos}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Imaginary Roots
questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+49y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(x)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+x{y}^{′}+49y=0,\,y(1)=2,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-1,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=2$ into the general solution gives

$$
2={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-1,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =7{x}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-1$ and ${c}_{1}=2$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-1 & =7{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{7}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=2\operatorname{cos}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x)-\frac{1}{7}\operatorname{sin}⁡(7\operatorname{ln}⁡x).
$$

questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+64y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y(t)={c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t),
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
{t}^{2}{y}^{″}+t{y}^{′}+64y=0,\,y(1)=3,\,{y}^{′}(1)=-2,\,t>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=3$ into the general solution gives

$$
3={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=-2,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =8\,{t}^{-1}({c}_{2}\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-{c}_{1}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t)).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=-2$ and ${c}_{1}=3$ into the above gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-2 & =8{c}_{2} \\ {c}_{2} & =-\frac{1}{4}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(t)=3\operatorname{cos}⁡(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t)-\frac{1}{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(8\operatorname{ln}⁡t).
$$

questions.knowledge_point: Solving an Initial Value Problem Involving a Cauchy-Euler Equation with Complex Roots
questions.problem:
Given that the differential equation

$$
5{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+25y=0
$$

has the general solution

$$
y=\frac{{c}_{1}\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+{c}_{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{x},
$$

solve the initial value problem

$$
5{x}^{2}{y}^{″}+15x{y}^{′}+25y=0,\,y(1)=1,\,{y}^{′}(1)=3,\,x>0.
$$
questions.worked_solution:
We find the constants ${c}_{1}$ and ${c}_{2}$ using the initial conditions.

- Substituting $y(1)=1$ into the general solution gives

$$
1={c}_{1}.
$$

- To apply the condition ${y}^{′}(1)=3,$ we first differentiate $y$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}(x) & =-{x}^{-2}(({c}_{1}-2{c}_{2})\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+(2{c}_{1}+{c}_{2})\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡(x))).\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we substitute ${y}^{′}(1)=3$ and ${c}_{1}=1$ into the above to get

$$
\begin{aligned}3 & =-(1-2{c}_{2}) \\ {c}_{2} & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the solution to the initial value problem is

$$
y(x)=\frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)+2\operatorname{sin}⁡(2\operatorname{ln}⁡x)}{x}.
$$
